# Course setup — tools for the MailGuard path

**Why this matters.** Security labs fail for boring reasons: wrong Python, no `venv`, Git missing, or tools installed too late. Without a repeatable machine baseline, every later module becomes “debug the laptop” instead of learning identity, email auth, and cloud access. On the job, the same hygiene — isolate deps, verify versions, defer heavy tooling until needed — keeps shared environments and CI honest.

**How it works.** Install a small **core** set now (Git, Python 3.11+, `venv`/`pip`, `pytest`, editor). Confirm each with a version check. Defer Node, Go, Docker, Terraform, kubectl/kind, and cloud CLIs until the module that needs them. That staged path mirrors how teams onboard: unblock day-one work first, then add platform tooling when the workload appears.

This module prepares your machine for the full course: identity / MFA katas, email authentication, Python APIs, TypeScript/Vue admin, Go workers, AWS/CI, Terraform, and local Kubernetes. You do **not** need every tool on day one — install **core** tools now, and the **later** tools when the matching module arrives.

Work through the installs below, then mark Module 00 complete on the site. This module has no assignment, quiz, or download pack.

---

## What the course uses (audit)

| Area | Tools / libraries | First needed |
|------|-------------------|--------------|
| Editor + VCS | Code editor; **Git** | 00 / whole course |
| Python path | **Python 3.11+**, `pip`, `venv`, **pytest**, **pyotp**, **cryptography**; later **FastAPI** | 01, 05, 07, 10 |
| Frontend | **Node.js** + npm/pnpm; **TypeScript**; **Vue 3**; optional **Svelte / SvelteKit** | 08, 17 (also to preview the course site: `cd site && npm start`) |
| Go path | **Go** toolchain (`go test`, modules) | 09 |
| Containers | **Docker** + **Docker Compose** | 12 (image CI step), 13, 14 |
| Cloud / CI | **GitHub** account; **GitHub Actions**; **AWS** account (free tier) or local stand-ins; **AWS CLI** (optional early) | 12+ |
| IaC | **Terraform** | 13 |
| Kubernetes | **kubectl**; **kind** or **minikube**; YAML / Helm or Kustomize; **Argo CD** for GitOps in 16 | 14–16 |
| Course site | Modern browser; Node.js to preview the site locally (`cd site && npm start`); later modules use fillable quiz PDFs | 00 / whole course |
| Sample data | Module fixtures and stubs in-repo (no separate dataset download) | per module |

Official docs linked below. Prefer current stable releases unless a module README pins a version.

---

## Core installs (do these now)

### 1. Git

Why: every module is a git-tracked lab; without Git you cannot pull fixes or keep `my-work/` history separate from course stubs.

- Windows: [Git for Windows](https://git-scm.com/download/win)
- macOS: [Git downloads](https://git-scm.com/download/mac) or `xcode-select --install`
- Linux: distro packages — e.g. `sudo apt install git` (Debian/Ubuntu)

**Check:** `git --version`

### 2. Python 3.11+ (or current stable 3.x)

Why: Challenge Gym and most identity/email katas are Python-first; an old or Store-alias interpreter breaks `venv` and pytest.

- Windows / macOS / source: [python.org downloads](https://www.python.org/downloads/)
- macOS (Homebrew): `brew install python`
- Linux: distro `python3` / `python3-venv` / `python3-pip`

On Windows installer, enable **Add python.exe to PATH**.

**Check:**

```bash
python3 --version   # Windows: py -3 --version  (or python --version)
python3 -m pip --version
```

On Windows use `py -3` (or `python`) instead of `python3`; `python3` may open the Microsoft Store alias.

### 3. Virtualenv + Challenge Gym deps

Why: a project `.venv` keeps course packages (`pyotp`, `cryptography`, pytest) off the system Python so CI and classmates get the same import graph.

From the course repo:

```bash
cd 01-challenge-gym
python3 -m venv .venv
# Windows PowerShell: py -3 -m venv .venv
# Windows PowerShell: .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
#   If activation is blocked: Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned
# Windows cmd.exe: .venv\Scripts\activate.bat
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
pytest -q
```

(Expect failing tests until you implement katas — the important part is that `pytest` runs. Why run it now: proves the toolchain, not that solutions exist yet.)

**Check:** `pytest --version`

### 4. Code editor

Any editor is fine (VS Code, Cursor, Neovim, etc.). Install a Python extension if you use VS Code/Cursor.

### 5. PDF reader for quizzes

Use a reader that can fill AcroForm PDFs (many browsers work; Preview / Adobe Reader / Okular also fine). Save finished PDFs under `my-work/quizzes/`.

---

## Install when you reach that module

### Node.js (Modules 08, 17)

- [Node.js LTS downloads](https://nodejs.org/)

**Check:** `node --version` · `npm --version`

### Go (Module 09)

- [Go install](https://go.dev/doc/install)

**Check:** `go version`

### Docker + Compose (Modules 13–14)

- [Docker Desktop](https://www.docker.com/products/docker-desktop/) (Windows/macOS) or [Docker Engine](https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/) (Linux)

**Check:** `docker --version` · `docker compose version`

### Terraform (Module 13)

- [HashiCorp Terraform installs](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/install)

**Check:** `terraform version`

### kubectl + kind or minikube (Modules 14–16)

- [kubectl install](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/tools/)
- [kind](https://kind.sigs.k8s.io/docs/user/quick-start/) or [minikube](https://minikube.sigs.k8s.io/docs/start/)

**Check:** `kubectl version --client` · `kind version` or `minikube version`

### GitHub + AWS (Modules 12+)

- [GitHub signup](https://github.com/signup)
- [AWS free tier](https://aws.amazon.com/free/) (or local stand-ins such as LocalStack/MinIO when a module allows)
- Optional: [AWS CLI](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/userguide/getting-started-install.html) — `aws --version`

Never commit cloud secrets. Module READMEs describe least-privilege demos.

---

## OS tips

| OS | Notes |
|----|--------|
| **Windows** | Prefer PowerShell or Git Bash; WSL2 is excellent for Python/Docker/kind. |
| **macOS** | Homebrew simplifies Git, Python, Go, Terraform, kubectl. |
| **Linux** | Use your distro packages for Git/Python; follow upstream docs for Docker/Terraform/kind. |

---

## Final setup checklist

Confirm each item before marking Module 00 complete:

1. `git --version` works  
2. `python3 --version` (Windows: `py -3 --version`) shows 3.11+ (or current stable 3.x)  
3. `python3 -m venv` (Windows: `py -3 -m venv`) works; Challenge Gym venv installs `requirements.txt`  
4. `pytest --version` works inside that venv  
5. Editor + Git configured; you can commit  
6. Browser opens the course site  
7. You know *when* to add Node, Go, Docker, Terraform, kubectl/kind, GitHub, and AWS  

Then mark Module 00 complete in the site progress UI. Next are short **language/tool primers** (Bash, then Python) before Module 01 — read-only like this setup module. Later primers appear immediately before the first module that uses that tool (SQL, TypeScript/Vue, Go, Docker, GitHub Actions, Terraform, Kubernetes YAML, Svelte).

# Bash / shell primer

**Why this matters.** Almost every MailGuard lab starts in a terminal: create a venv, run `pytest`, call `go test`, or bring Compose up. Without shell fluency, the “how” of every later module stays blocked behind copy-paste. On the job, the same skill lets you reproduce CI failures, inspect logs, and keep secrets in the environment instead of committed files.

**How it works.** A shell reads a line, expands variables/globs, then runs a program. Pipes (`|`) pass stdout of one command to stdin of the next. Environment variables configure tools without hard-coding secrets into files you might commit. Exit codes (`$?` / `$LASTEXITCODE`) are how scripts and pipelines decide pass vs fail.

This primer has no assignment, quiz, or download pack — read, try the tiny example, mark complete, then continue.

---

## What Bash is

**Bash** (Bourne Again SHell) is a command language common on Linux/macOS. On Windows, **Git Bash**, **WSL**, or **PowerShell** cover the same lab ideas with slightly different syntax.

## Why industry uses it

Cloud and security work is automation-heavy: CI runners, remote bastions, and container entrypoints are shell-first. Guis help explore; shells make steps repeatable and reviewable in git.

## Key concepts for upcoming labs

| Concept | Why you care |
|---------|----------------|
| `cd` / paths | Every module README assumes you are in the right folder |
| `export VAR=…` | Tokens and API URLs stay out of source when possible |
| pipes / redirects | Compose logs, `pytest -q`, filtering output |
| exit codes | Scripts and CI fail when a command returns non-zero |

## Install / open a shell

- **macOS / Linux:** Terminal.app, iTerm, or your desktop terminal — Bash or zsh both work for this course.
- **Windows:** [Git for Windows](https://git-scm.com/download/win) (Git Bash), [WSL2](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/install), or PowerShell (`py -3`, `python`, etc. as Module 00 notes).

**Check:** `echo $SHELL` (Git Bash/WSL/macOS/Linux) or `$PSVersionTable` in PowerShell.

## Tiny hands-on example

```bash
# Why: confirm the shell runs commands and prints exit status
mkdir -p /tmp/mailguard-shell-demo && cd /tmp/mailguard-shell-demo
echo "hold" > decision.txt
grep -n hold decision.txt && echo "exit was $?"
```

**How:** `mkdir` creates a sandbox, `echo` writes a file, `grep` searches it, `$?` shows the last exit code — the same pattern CI uses to fail a job.

## Official docs

1. [GNU Bash manual](https://www.gnu.org/software/bash/manual/)
2. [Git for Windows](https://gitforwindows.org/)
3. [PowerShell docs](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/)

---

## Done when

You can explain **why** this tool shows up on the MailGuard path and **how** to install/run the tiny example. Mark this primer complete on the site, then continue to the next module (`01-challenge-gym`).

This primer has **no** assignment, quiz, or download pack.

# Python primer

**Why this matters.** MailGuard’s identity, email-auth, API, and capstone labs are Python-first. Without a working interpreter, venv, and pytest habit, Challenge Gym cannot prove the “how” behind TOTP, holds, and rules. On the job, the same loop — isolate deps, let tests define the contract — is how teams ship auth and email-security glue without “works on my machine.”

**How it works.** You isolate deps in a **virtual environment**, install from `requirements.txt`, implement stubs under `katas/`, and let **pytest** define the contract. That loop (read test → write code → re-run) is the course’s core practice: fail first, then make the stub match the spec.

This primer has no assignment, quiz, or download pack.

---

## What Python is

**Python** is a high-level language widely used for APIs, automation, and security tooling. This course targets **Python 3.11+** (or current stable 3.x).

## Why industry uses it

Teams choose Python for fast iteration on auth, data, and glue code: readable modules, rich libraries (`cryptography`, web frameworks), and excellent test ergonomics. Cloud-security prototypes often start here before hardening.

## Key concepts for Module 01+

| Concept | Why you care |
|---------|----------------|
| `venv` | Keeps course deps from fighting system Python |
| `pip install -r requirements.txt` | Reproducible lab installs |
| functions + type hints (light) | Clear kata stubs |
| `pytest` | Tests are the spec — fail first, then implement |

## Install and run

Follow Module 00 if needed, then:

```bash
# Why: confirm 3.x, then isolate this primer’s deps from system site-packages
python3 --version   # Windows: py -3 --version
python3 -m venv /tmp/mg-py-primer && source /tmp/mg-py-primer/bin/activate
# Windows PowerShell: py -3 -m venv .venv ; .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
```

Official install: [python.org downloads](https://www.python.org/downloads/).

## Tiny hands-on example

```bash
cat > /tmp/mg_hello.py << 'EOF'
def hold_reason(score: int) -> str:
    # Why: small pure function — easy to unit test later
    return "hold" if score >= 80 else "allow"

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(hold_reason(90))
EOF
python /tmp/mg_hello.py
```

**How:** A pure function returns a decision string — the same shape as later hold-rule katas, without frameworks yet.

## Official docs

1. [Python 3 tutorial](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/)
2. [venv docs](https://docs.python.org/3/library/venv.html)
3. [pytest documentation](https://docs.pytest.org/)

---

## Done when

You can explain **why** this tool shows up on the MailGuard path and **how** to install/run the tiny example. Mark this primer complete on the site, then continue to the next module (`01-challenge-gym`).

This primer has **no** assignment, quiz, or download pack.

# Reading — Basic auth JSON client

## Learning objectives

1. Build an HTTP Basic `Authorization` header (RFC 7617).
2. Parse a minimal JSON token response safely.
3. Reason about clock skew when pairing auth with TOTP.

**Why this matters.** Many lab and legacy APIs still gate calls with HTTP Basic. Without understanding how the header is built — and why cleartext HTTP fails — you either leak credentials or silently accept broken token JSON. On the job, pairing Basic (or any password-bearing header) with TOTP and clock-skew checks is a common “authenticated client + MFA” interview and integration pattern.

**How it works.** Form the credential string as `username:password`, Base64-encode that **single** string, and send `Authorization: Basic <encoded>` (RFC 7617). Over TLS only — Base64 is encoding, not encryption. Parse the JSON body as an object and require an explicit `token` (fail closed if missing). When the same client also verifies TOTP, compare client/server Unix time against a `max_skew` budget so modest clock drift does not look like an attack.

## Read these (verified)

1. [RFC 7617](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7617)
2. [MDN — Authorization](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Authorization)
3. [httpx Auth](https://www.python-httpx.org/advanced/authentication/) or [requests Auth](https://requests.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user/authentication/)

## Next step

Assignment → `katas/basic_auth_client.py` → quiz.

# Reading — Crypto hygiene

## Learning objectives

By the end of this kata’s reading + assignment + implementation, you should be able to:

1. Explain why a bare hash is the wrong tool for message **integrity** when an attacker can modify bytes — and why Hash-based Message Authentication Code (**HMAC**) binds a secret key to the hash.
2. Describe Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (**AEAD**) as “encrypt + authenticate in one construction,” and name Transport Layer Security (**TLS**) as the everyday place AEAD (and certificates) show up.
3. State a short **key lifecycle** checklist (generate, store, rotate, revoke) and refuse to invent ciphers — use reviewed libraries instead.

**Why this matters.** A bare hash looks like “integrity” until an attacker rewrites both the bytes and the digest. Without keyed integrity (HMAC) or authenticated encryption (AEAD), webhooks, audit blobs, and secrets-at-rest can be forged or silently altered. On the job, TLS already uses AEAD for every hop you trust — the same misuse rules (nonce reuse, inventing ciphers, skipping auth) show up in application crypto for email and identity services.

**How it works.** **HMAC** binds a secret key to a hash so only key holders can produce a valid tag; verify with constant-time compare. **AEAD** (e.g. AES-GCM) encrypts and authenticates in one construction; associated data is authenticated but not encrypted. Prefer reviewed libraries (`hmac`, `cryptography.AESGCM`). Key lifecycle: generate (CSPRNG) → store outside git → rotate → revoke. Never reuse a nonce with the same key.

![Comparison of bare hash, HMAC, and AEAD plus a generate-store-rotate-revoke key lifecycle](images/crypto-hygiene.svg)

*Figure. A bare hash is not authenticity when an attacker can change bytes; **HMAC** binds a secret key; **AEAD** encrypts and authenticates together (TLS is the everyday place this shows up). Notice the key lifecycle strip — generate, store, rotate, revoke — and the rule to use reviewed libraries. Original course diagram (CC0).*

**TLS** (Transport Layer Security) is the protocol that protects HTTP and SMTP connections: the server presents an X.509 **certificate** (a signed binding of public key ↔ name), the client verifies the chain to a trusted root, then the peers agree on a cipher suite. TLS 1.3 uses only AEAD suites (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305); TLS 1.2 also allowed non-AEAD CBC suites. You will not implement TLS here; you *will* practice the same misuse rules TLS libraries already enforce — never reuse a nonce with the same key, never skip authentication, never treat “encrypt with raw AES-ECB” as done.

## Videos (verified)

1. **[Public Key Cryptography - Computerphile](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GSIDS_lvRv4)** — Computerphile (feat. Dr Mike Pound)  
   Why it helps: mental model for public/private keys before certificates feel magical.

2. **[TLS Handshake Explained](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=86cQJ0MMses)** — Computerphile (feat. Dr Mike Pound)  
   Why it helps: certificate check → key agreement → encrypted application data, without drowning in RFCs. Written companion: [Cloudflare Learning — What happens in a TLS handshake?](https://www.cloudflare.com/learning/ssl/what-happens-in-a-tls-handshake/).

3. **[AES Explained (Advanced Encryption Standard)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=O4xNJsjtN6E)** — Computerphile (feat. Dr Mike Pound)  
   Why it helps: intuition for the block cipher under AES-GCM — then remember this kata uses **AEAD** (GCM), not raw ECB.

## Read these (verified)

### Specs & libraries

1. [RFC 2104 — HMAC](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc2104) — keyed hashing for integrity/authenticity.
2. [Python `hmac` — cryptographic message authentication](https://docs.python.org/3/library/hmac.html) — `hmac.new`, `compare_digest`.
3. [PyCA cryptography — AESGCM](https://cryptography.io/en/latest/hazmat/primitives/aead/#cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead.AESGCM) — AEAD seal/open API you will call.

### Concepts & security literacy

4. [OWASP Cryptographic Storage Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Cryptographic_Storage_Cheat_Sheet.html) — algorithms, key management, common failures.
5. [MDN — Transport Layer Security (TLS)](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Security/Transport_Layer_Security) — what browsers verify and why mixed content breaks the model.
6. [Latacora — Cryptographic Right Answers](https://www.latacora.com/blog/2018/04/03/cryptographic-right-answers/) — opinionated “what to use” list (pair with current library docs).

### Why this kata exists (career prep)

7. Cloud security SaaS work expects engineers to *consume* crypto correctly (TLS termination, secret storage, HMAC webhooks) — not invent primitives.
8. MailGuard’s audit and secure-transfer paths need integrity and confidentiality literacy even when the product story is DLP, not a crypto product.

## Optional deepeners

- [NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev. 5 — Recommendation for Key Management](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/57/pt1/r5/final) — lifecycle vocabulary (generate, distribute, store, rotate, destroy).
- Skim certificate fields in a browser’s certificate viewer once after the kata is green.

## Next step

Continue with the assignment from the downloads on this page. The quiz is required after you attempt the assignment and tests.

# Reading — Hold rules

## Learning objectives

By the end of this kata’s reading + assignment + implementation, you should be able to:

1. Describe email Data Loss Prevention (DLP) as ordered policy: match conditions → action (allow / hold-suspend / reject-discard).
2. Implement **first-match-wins** evaluation over a small rule list without inventing a Domain-Specific Language (DSL).
3. Connect the toy engine to real product language (Microsoft Purview / Google Workspace DLP and similar SaaS email guards) so you can explain trade-offs in an interview.

**Why this matters.** Without outbound policy, sensitive mail leaves the org the moment someone hits Send — autocomplete mistakes and rushed CCs are expensive. Email Data Loss Prevention (DLP) exists so messages are inspected and acted on *before* delivery. On the job, SaaS email guards and security gateways all share the same inspect → match → act shape; this kata trains that vocabulary without a product lock-in.

**How it works.** An ordered rule list runs against each message. Each rule has predicates (recipient domain, substring in subject/body) and an action (**allow**, **hold/suspend**, **reject/discard**). Evaluation is **first-match-wins**: stop at the first matching rule. Order *is* policy. This kata keeps predicates tiny and skips inventing a DSL so the engine stays interview-explainable.

![Ordered hold rules evaluating a message with first-match-wins allow, hold, or reject outcomes](images/hold-rules-flow.svg)

*Figure. Inspect the message, walk the ordered rule list, and stop at the **first match**. Notice the three actions — allow, hold/suspend, reject/discard — and that evaluation order is part of the policy, not an afterthought. Original course diagram (CC0).*

Real email DLP products share this shape: rules that allow, suspend, or discard to prevent costly mis-sends of sensitive information. MailGuard later folders reuse the same allow / hold / reject vocabulary.

## Videos (verified)

1. **[What is Data Loss Prevention (DLP)?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=meWpZCmV0dg)** — Google Workspace  
   Why it helps: short official intro to DLP as **rules** that scan content and enforce an action when a rule matches.

2. **[Data Loss Prevention across endpoints, apps, & services | Microsoft Purview](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hvqq8L_0kgI)** — Microsoft Mechanics  
   Why it helps: shows how one DLP policy idea spans email and other channels — same “inspect → match → act” loop as this kata, at product scale.

3. **[Plan and design Data Loss Prevention (DLP) Policies | SC-401 | Episode 5](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Agp8I97XHlk)** — Microsoft Learn  
   Why it helps: policy design (what to monitor, where, conditions, actions) maps cleanly onto ordered hold/allow/reject rules.

## Read these (verified)

### Product / domain context

1. [What is Data Loss Prevention (DLP)? — Google Workspace](https://support.google.com/a/answer/9646351) — rules that scan content and enforce actions.
2. [Microsoft Purview Data Loss Prevention](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/purview/dlp-learn-about-dlp) — protection, detection, and response framing for email and sharing.
3. Challenge bar for this kata: short, elegant solutions — keep the engine interview-explainable.

### Engineering craft for this kata

4. [Python `dataclasses`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/dataclasses.html) — frozen message/rule records as used in the stub.
5. [pytest — Get Started](https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/getting-started.html) — tests are the contract; run them often.

### Missend / privacy literacy (why “hold” exists)

6. [NZ Privacy Commissioner — prevent privacy breaches through email](https://www.privacy.org.nz/resources-and-learning/knowledge-base/view/516/) — wrong recipient is a top reported breach; check recipients; delays/reminders help.
7. [OVIC — tips to reduce data breaches when sending emails](https://ovic.vic.gov.au/privacy/resources-for-organisations/tips-to-reduce-data-breaches-when-sending-emails/) — human error, verify full addresses, delay-send patterns.

## Keep in mind

Production DLP adds attachment inspection, admin UX, queues, and richer matching. Your kata stays dumb on purpose — interview-explainable order and predicates first. Later MailGuard folders (API, Go workers, Vue admin, AWS) extend this toy engine toward a fuller SaaS shape.

## Next step

Continue with the assignment from the downloads on this page. The quiz is required after you attempt the assignment and tests.

# Reading — Recipient risk

## Learning objectives

By the end of this kata’s reading + assignment + implementation, you should be able to:

1. Classify recipients as internal / external / invalid against an org domain after simple normalization.
2. Explain why **mixed** or **invalid** recipient sets are a missend / data-loss signal that can feed a hold rule.
3. Distinguish accidental missends from **Business Email Compromise (BEC)** / phishing — same “verify the recipient” habit, different attacker model.

**Why this matters.** Accidental missends (internal + external in one To/Cc) and invalid addresses leak data or bounce into the wrong inbox. Without a recipient-risk signal, hold rules have nothing principled to trigger on. On the job, the same “verify the recipient” habit shows up in DLP products and in Business Email Compromise (BEC) playbooks — different attacker models, same classification step.

**How it works.** Normalize each address (strip, lowercase domain), then classify as **internal**, **external**, or **invalid** against the org domain. A set that is **mixed** or contains **invalid** addresses is a missend / data-loss signal that can feed a hold rule. # Reading — Parametrized TOTP (RFC 6238)

## Learning objectives

1. Implement HOTP dynamic truncation (RFC 4226 §5.3) yourself.
2. Parametrize TOTP by digest (SHA-1/256/512), digits (6–10), step, and T0.
3. Validate against RFC 6238 Appendix B vectors and the errata on seed lengths.
4. Optionally port the same logic to Go (`crypto/hmac`, `encoding/binary`).

**Why this matters.** Library wrappers are fine for product MFA — but screening-style tasks (and debugging interop) often require you to **derive the counter, HMAC, and truncate** correctly. Without the RFC 6238 errata on seed lengths, SHA-256/512 vectors fail mysteriously even when truncation looks right. On the job, knowing *how* TOTP is built helps you validate vendor libraries and clock-skew edge cases instead of treating OTP as a black box.

**How it works.** Counter `T = floor((t − T0) / X)` (X usually 30s). HMAC the 8-byte big-endian counter with the shared secret. Dynamic truncation (RFC 4226 §5.3): offset from the **last** HMAC byte’s low nibble; take four bytes; clear the high bit (`& 0x7F`); reduce mod `10^digits`. Appendix B publishes known answers; the errata requires seed length to match the hash (20 / 32 / 64 bytes), not one 20-byte seed for every digest.

## Short note

Pair this with the Basic-auth JSON client kata when you need an authenticated call that also tolerates small clock skew.

## Read these (verified)

1. [RFC 4226 — HOTP](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4226) — §5.3 truncation.
2. [RFC 6238 — TOTP](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6238) — §4 + Appendix B.
3. [RFC 6238 errata](https://www.rfc-editor.org/errata_search.php?rfc=6238) — seed length per hash.
4. [RFC 7617 — HTTP Basic](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7617) — Authorization header.

## Keep in mind

Never paste employer challenge text into public repos. Publish only your own generic implementation and keep secrets out of gists.

# Reading — TOTP verify

## Learning objectives

By the end of this kata’s reading + assignment + implementation, you should be able to:

1. Explain Time-based One-Time Password (TOTP) as HMAC-based One-Time Password (HOTP) with a time-derived counter (shared secret + time step → short code).
2. State why a small verification **window** exists (clock skew) and what it does *not* replace (rate limits, replay controls).
3. Verify codes with `pyotp` instead of hand-rolling Hash-based Message Authentication Code (HMAC) — and point to RFC 6238 / Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) literacy in an interview.

**Why this matters.** Passwords alone fail when credentials leak or phishing succeeds. TOTP adds a second factor so a stolen password is not enough — but without understanding clock skew, replay, and why you should not hand-roll HMAC, MFA implementations break users or invent bugs. On the job, identity and email-security products expect this literacy when you wire MFA into admin consoles and APIs.

**How it works.** Server and authenticator share a secret **K**. Both derive counter **T** from Unix time ÷ step (usually 30s), run HMAC, truncate to a short code, and compare. A small verify **window** accepts ±N neighboring steps for clock skew only — it does not replace rate limits or replay tracking. Prefer `pyotp` over reinventing crypto; production controls (replay store, lockout, secret-at-rest) land later in `02-mailguard-mfa/`.

![TOTP flow from shared secret and time counter through HMAC to a short code, with a server verification window](images/totp-flow.svg)

*Figure. Shared secret **K** and time counter **T** feed HMAC; truncation yields the short code both the app and server compute. The verify **window** only covers clock skew — notice it does not replace rate limits or replay controls. Original course diagram (CC0).*

# Reading — Passkeys / WebAuthn (beside TOTP MFA)

## Learning objectives

1. Explain **Web Authentication (WebAuthn)** as a browser API for public-key credentials scoped to a relying-party **RP ID** (a registrable domain suffix), not exactly the full origin string alone.
2. Contrast phishing risk of **TOTP** (user can type a code into a fake site) vs **passkeys** (origin-bound assertion).
3. Place passkeys next to MailGuard’s TOTP path as a *next* factor — not a rewrite of Challenge Gym.

**Why this matters.** TOTP proves “something you have,” but a convincing phishing page can still harvest the live code and replay it. Without phishing-resistant authenticators, identity and cloud admin portals stay one lookalike domain away from account takeover. On the job, passkeys / WebAuthn are how teams raise assurance beside (or instead of) OTP — without claiming TOTP literacy alone is enough.

**How it works.** At registration, the authenticator creates a public-key credential bound to the relying-party **RP ID**. At assertion, the browser/OS signs a server challenge only for that RP ID / origin. A lookalike domain should not get a usable assertion. Recovery (lost device, backup passkey, IT-assisted reset) is an operational design problem — plan it before turning off TOTP/recovery codes.

# Reading — Identity depth (SAML, device certs, password managers)

## Learning objectives

1. Compare **SAML** and **OIDC** for enterprise single sign-on (**SSO**) at a high level.
2. Explain device certificates / posture as *additional signals*, not magic.
3. Threat-model an enterprise password manager for apps that still use passwords (non-SSO).

**Why this matters.** Enterprises rarely run “OIDC only.” Without SAML literacy, device-posture signals, and a threat model for password managers on non-SSO apps, identity work stops at the happy path and fails in real estates of legacy apps. # Reading — SAML 2.0 + OIDC lab deepen

## Learning objectives

1. Run **Keycloak** locally as an IdP (lab only).
2. Contrast auth-code + **PKCE** (OIDC) with SAML SP/IdP-initiated flows.
3. Check assertion conditions: audience, recipient/ACS, time window, InResponseTo, signature present.
4. Know headline attacks: XML Signature Wrapping, unsigned assertions, open redirects; OAuth mix-up / redirect URI mismatch.

**Why this matters.** Federation bugs are not theoretical: unsigned assertions, loose ACS/redirect matching, and missing PKCE turn “we have SSO” into account takeover. Without checking audience, time windows, and InResponseTo, replay and mix-up attacks succeed. On the job, identity engineers validate these conditions every time a new app joins the IdP.

## Learning objectives

1. Define **Zero Trust** as “never trust, always verify” with continuous evaluation — not a single product SKU.
2. Contrast network-level **VPN** admission with application-level **ZTNA**.
3. Name Policy Engine / Policy Enforcement Point ideas from National Institute of Standards and Technology (**NIST**) SP 800-207 at a high level.

**Why this matters.** Classical VPN admission parks a client on a flat corporate LAN. After credential theft or malware, **lateral movement** reaches many internal services. # Reading — Email authentication & SMTP/TLS literacy

## Learning objectives

1. Explain Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (**SMTP**) as the store-and-forward *sending* protocol, and why Transport Layer Security (**TLS**) on SMTP encrypts a hop but does **not** by itself prove the `From:` domain is legitimate. Server-to-server STARTTLS is **opportunistic**: an active attacker can strip it, and certificates are often not validated. **MTA-STS** (RFC 8461) or **DANE** (RFC 7672) make TLS required and authenticated for a receiving domain, and **TLS-RPT** (RFC 8460) reports failures. Implicit TLS (port 465) applies to client submission (RFC 8314), not MX-to-MX.
2. Distinguish Sender Policy Framework (**SPF**), DomainKeys Identified Mail (**DKIM**), and Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance (**DMARC**) — what each checks and how they combine. DMARC passes if **at least one** of SPF or DKIM passes **and** aligns with the visible `From:`.
3. Read a DMARC DNS policy (`p=`, `rua=`, and RFC 9989 tags such as `t=` / `np=` / `psd=`) and say what hold/DLP rules **cannot** fix alone when attackers spoof lookalike mail.

**Why this matters.** Hold/DLP rules catch *outbound* mistakes; they do not stop attackers who **spoof** your (or a partner’s) domain into someone else’s inbox. Without SPF/DKIM/DMARC, receivers cannot tell authorized mail from lookalike fraud. On the job, email and cloud-security teams publish DNS auth, read aggregate reports, and step `p=` carefully — TLS on SMTP encrypts a hop but does not prove `From:`.

**How it works.** **SMTP** forwards mail hop-by-hop; TLS on a hop encrypts that connection (STARTTLS between MTAs is opportunistic unless MTA-STS/DANE enforce it). **SPF** lists hosts allowed for the envelope sender / HELO — not the header `From:`. **DKIM** signs selected headers/body; public key in DNS. **DMARC** requires SPF or DKIM to **pass and align** with the visible `From:`, sets policy (`p=`), and collects reports (`rua`). Receivers combine these; operators use reports before flipping to `p=reject`.

![SPF, DKIM, and DMARC checks from sending MTA through receiving MTA with DNS-published controls](images/spf-dkim-dmarc.svg)

*Figure. SMTP+TLS protects the hop; **SPF** authorizes envelope hosts, **DKIM** signs content, **DMARC** aligns results with the visible `From:` and sets `p=` policy. Notice hold/DLP and domain auth solve different problems (outbound mistakes vs inbound spoof). Original course diagram (CC0).*

## Videos (verified)

1. **[SPF, DKIM and DMARC Protocols Explained](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eR6996cQvY)** — PowerDMARC  
   Why it helps: end-to-end picture of the three DNS-published controls receivers combine.

2. **[Email Trust and Antispoofing: DKIM, SPF, and DMARC](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZFg691hXDzk)** — Salesforce Support  
   Why it helps: operator-oriented setup narrative (`p=none` → stricter policies) without requiring their product.

3. **[Set up email authentication](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YdWgHAcD91E)** — Google Workspace  
   Why it helps: SPF/DKIM publish steps and where DMARC fits for modern receivers.

## Read these (verified)

1. [RFC 7208 — SPF](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7208) — skim abstract + mechanism overview (MAIL FROM / HELO identity).
2. [RFC 6376 — DKIM](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6376) — signature + public key in DNS.
3. [RFC 9989 — DMARC](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9989) — current protocol (Standards Track; obsoletes RFC 7489 and RFC 9091). Companion: [RFC 9990](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9990) (aggregate reports), [RFC 9991](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9991) (failure reports). RFC 9989 removes `pct`/`rf`/`ri` and adds `t` (test mode), `np`, and `psd`; the Public Suffix List is replaced by a DNS tree walk.
4. [DMARC.org overview](https://dmarc.org/overview/) — plain-language diagram.
5. [Cloudflare Learning — What are DMARC, DKIM, and SPF?](https://www.cloudflare.com/learning/email-security/dmarc-dkim-spf/) — concise comparison.
6. [Google — Email sender guidelines](https://support.google.com/a/answer/81126) — modern receiver expectations (SPF/DKIM/DMARC).
7. [Cloudflare Learning — What is SMTP?](https://www.cloudflare.com/learning/email-security/what-is-smtp/) — SMTP + why encryption ≠ authentication.
8. [RFC 8461 — MTA-STS](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8461) · [RFC 8460 — TLS-RPT](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8460) · [RFC 7672 — DANE for SMTP](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7672) — authenticated/required SMTP TLS and failure reporting.

### Aggregate reports (DMARC report literacy)

Receivers email XML **aggregate reports** to `rua=` addresses summarizing pass/fail by source IP. Operators use them to find legitimate senders missing SPF/DKIM (or alignment) before flipping `p=reject`. This course does not require a live domain — parse policies in the kata and describe what a report would tell you on the assignment.

# Reading — Mail flow + DMARC aggregate analytics

## Learning objectives

1. Place a cloud **email security gateway** relative to Microsoft 365 / Google Workspace (MX vs outbound smart-host).
2. Explain connectors/transport rules, journaling/archive, ARC (RFC 8617), and why SPF often fails after relay while DMARC may still pass via DKIM.
3. Parse DMARC aggregate reports (RFC 9990-shaped) and recommend the next `p=` step.
4. Know bulk-sender receiver mandates (Google/Yahoo 2024; Outlook.com high-volume expectations).

**Why this matters.** Real mail rarely goes “MUA → final MX” in one hop. Gateways, relays, and journaling rewrite paths so SPF breaks even for legitimate senders — and without aggregate analytics you either stay on `p=none` forever or flip to `p=reject` and break payroll/marketing. On the job, email-security engineers read RFC 9990-shaped reports, preserve DKIM (or ARC), and place MX vs outbound smart-hosts deliberately.

**How it works.** **Inbound:** MX points at the gateway (or workspace); mail is inspected then delivered. **Outbound:** workspace sends via a smart-host/gateway that may rewrite envelope data — SPF often fails after relay, while aligned **DKIM** can still make **DMARC** pass. **ARC** (RFC 8617) helps downstream receivers trust authentication results across intermediaries. Aggregate reports summarize pass/fail by source IP so you climb `none → quarantine → reject` with evidence. Bulk-sender mandates expect SPF/DKIM/DMARC at minimum.

# Reading — Threat modeling & lightweight secure SDLC

## Learning objectives

1. Apply a **STRIDE**-lite pass to MailGuard’s hold/release path (who can spoof an operator? tamper with rules? deny the queue?).
2. Relate findings to mitigations you already ship (MFA, audit logs, first-match rules, CI) and gaps you document honestly.
3. Skim **OWASP SAMM** as a maturity *map*, not a certificate — pick one practice to improve next.

**Why this matters.** Shipping hold/release without naming abuse stories leaves gaps that MFA, audits, and CI cannot invent for you. Teams that skip threat modeling discover spoofed operators, silent rule tampering, and held-body disclosure in production — after users are affected. A lightweight pass costs a page of Markdown; a missed elevation path costs incident response.

**How it works.** Threat modeling asks four questions (Shostack): what are we working on → what can go wrong → what are we doing about it → did we do a good job? **STRIDE** (Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege) is a Microsoft-origin checklist that maps each abuse story to a concrete element (session, rule store, queue). Secure Software Development Life Cycle (**SDLC**) means those questions recur in requirements, design, implementation, test, and operate — not only in a final pen-test fantasy. **LINDDUN** is a privacy-oriented sibling; for MailGuard, focus on disclosure of held message bodies and audit access. **OWASP SAMM** (Software Assurance Maturity Model) maps five business functions (Governance, Design, Implementation, Verification, Operations) so you pick *one* practice to improve — not claim enterprise maturity.

**On the job.** Email and identity gateways always have privileged operator actions (release, rule edit). Interviewers and security reviews expect you to walk a trust-boundary diagram and name STRIDE rows with mitigations or honest gaps — vendor-neutral vocabulary that transfers across cloud mail and SaaS admin consoles.

## Short intro

Threat modeling asks “what can go wrong?” before or while you build. Secure Software Development Life Cycle (**SDLC**) means security activities show up in requirements, design, implementation, test, and operate — not only in a final pen-test fantasy.

**STRIDE** is still useful interview vocabulary. Prefer a short table over a unused enterprise tool: six abuse stories tied to MailGuard’s hold path beat a blank “we follow best practices.”

![STRIDE-lite checklist with example questions for a hold and release path](images/stride-lite.svg)

*Figure. Six STRIDE categories as a lightweight checklist on the hold/release path. Notice each tile pairs a threat question with a mitigation you may already ship (MFA, audit logs, least privilege) — document gaps honestly. Original course diagram (CC0).*

| Approach | When it helps | Cost / limit |
|----------|---------------|--------------|
| STRIDE-lite table | Fast feature reviews | Misses privacy-specific linking threats (use LINDDUN-lite) |

# SQL primer

**Why this matters.** Hold/release queues need **durable** state: who held a message, when, and whether it was released. In-memory demos lose that story on restart; without a queryable store you cannot prove “who released this hold?” after an incident. Document stores or logs alone rarely give the same transactional constraints for account/rule/audit rows — SQL remains the default for that shape of SaaS data.

**How it works.** You model entities as **tables** (rows + columns), identify rows with **keys**, and change data with declarative statements (`SELECT` / `INSERT` / `UPDATE`). The MailGuard API module starts in-memory, then asks you to *sketch* a Postgres-shaped design — this primer is that vocabulary. On the job, the same pattern backs email-security and identity APIs: durable holds, rules, and audit trails operators can query.

This primer has no assignment, quiz, or download pack.

---

## What SQL is

**SQL** (Structured Query Language) is the standard language for relational databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, and cloud variants).

## Why industry uses it

Relational stores give strong consistency for account, rule, and audit data. Security products lean on queryable audit trails — “who released this hold?” — which tables express well.

## Key concepts for Module 07

| Concept | Why you care |
|---------|----------------|
| Primary key | Stable id for a held message |
| NOT NULL / constraints | Reject impossible states early |
| `SELECT` / `INSERT` / `UPDATE` | Read and mutate hold rows |
| Migrations (awareness) | Schema changes ship with app versions (Alembic later) |

## Install and run

You do **not** need a live database for this primer — the vocabulary above is enough to start Module 07. Optional (why: muscle memory for `psql` / SQLite before the stretch persistence lab): install [PostgreSQL](https://www.postgresql.org/download/) or use SQLite for experiments. Module 07 keeps the kata in-memory; persistence is a stretch with SQLAlchemy/Alembic links in readings.

## Tiny hands-on example

```sql
-- Why: one table can answer "what is held?" without an app server
CREATE TABLE holds (
  id          TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  state       TEXT NOT NULL,  -- held | released | rejected
  created_at  TEXT NOT NULL,
  actor       TEXT NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO holds (id, state, created_at, actor)
VALUES ('msg-1', 'held', '2026-11-13T12:00:00Z', 'api');

SELECT id, state FROM holds WHERE state = 'held';
```

**How:** `CREATE TABLE` defines the shape; `INSERT` records a hold; `SELECT` filters — the same questions operators ask in an admin UI.

## Official docs

1. [PostgreSQL documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/)
2. [SQLAlchemy ORM quick start](https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/20/orm/quickstart.html) (stretch after Module 07)
3. [Alembic tutorial](https://alembic.sqlalchemy.org/en/latest/tutorial.html)

---

## Done when

You can explain **why** this tool shows up on the MailGuard path and **how** to install/run the tiny example. Mark this primer complete on the site, then continue to the next module (`07-mailguard-api`).

This primer has **no** assignment, quiz, or download pack.

# Reading — Hold / approve / release

## Learning objectives

1. Model a first-class hold queue with explicit state transitions.
2. Separate **approve** (human decision) from **release** (send onward).
3. Reject illegal transitions instead of silently no-oping.

**Why this matters.** Collapsing “approve” and “release” into one click is how held mail leaves without a recorded human decision — or how a bug silently no-ops and operators think work finished. Illegal transitions that return 200 hide missends. Explicit states (`held` → `approved` → `released`, or `rejected`) exist so audits answer “who decided?” separately from “did it leave?”

**How it works.** A hold starts **held**. An operator **approves** (policy OK) or **rejects**. Only **approved** items may **release** to the next hop. The API rejects jumps (e.g. held → released) with a client error (often 409). Stretch: persist rows in Postgres via SQLAlchemy; **Alembic** migrations version the schema so deploys do not hand-edit production tables. Auto-bcc / delete-on-condition are explicit **action kinds**, not silent side effects of allow — so least privilege and audit stay possible.

```
held --approve--> approved --release--> released
  \--reject--> rejected
```

**On the job.** Every email-security and DLP review queue uses a similar state machine. Cloud identity/admin tools likewise separate “decision recorded” from “side effect executed.” Being able to draw the diagram and defend illegal-transition errors is day-one literacy for gateway work.

## Short intro

An email-security gateway often **holds** outbound mail for review. Operators approve or reject; only approved items are released to the next hop. Keep vocabulary vendor-neutral: hold, approve, release, reject.

Persistence (Postgres + SQLAlchemy/Alembic) belongs in your stretch lab — the kata stays a pure state machine you can unit-test.

# Reading — MailGuard API

## Learning objectives

1. Sketch a small HTTP API that stores ordered hold/allow/reject rules.
2. Evaluate a message against those rules with **first-match-wins** semantics.
3. Cover happy path and edge cases with automated tests.

**Why this matters.** Without a rules API, operators cannot encode “hold external domains” or “reject secret substrings” as durable policy — every decision becomes a one-off script. First-match-wins without tests drifts into silent allow; an in-memory-only store vanishes on restart and cannot support multi-instance or audit. History of mail gateways is full of policy engines that grew from ad-hoc filters; a thin, tested evaluate function is the trade-off that keeps the kata honest before Postgres and authn.

**How it works.** Operators **create** ordered rules (predicates + decision). On evaluate, the service walks the list top-down, stops at the **first** match, and returns `hold` / `allow` / `reject` (or a documented default). Keep evaluation as a **pure function** separate from FastAPI handlers so pytest can cover edge cases without HTTP. Pydantic models shape requests; OpenAPI documents the surface. Persistence, authn/z, and pagination stay out of the kata on purpose — stretch labs add Postgres later.

```
Client → POST /rules  → store (ordered list)
Client → POST /evaluate(message) → walk rules → first match → decision
```

**On the job.** Email DLP and identity-adjacent gateways expose the same pattern: policy CRUD + evaluate on the message path. Interviewers care that you can explain first-match vs scoring, why pure evaluation is testable, and what an in-memory store cannot prove in production — vendor-neutral skills for any cloud mail or SaaS security API.

## Short intro

MailGuard’s product thread needs a **rules API**: operators create rules; the service decides whether an outbound message is allowed, held for review, or rejected. This module is a thin FastAPI-shaped service with an in-memory store and a pure evaluation function you can unit-test without standing up a database.

Keep the public vocabulary vendor-neutral: rules, holds, allow, reject — not a commercial product clone.

4. Challenge Gym [`hold_rules`](../../01-challenge-gym/readings/hold_rules.md) — same decision vocabulary.

## Keep in mind

Production APIs add authn/z, persistence, pagination, and audit logs. Your kata stays small on purpose — **why:** prove the decision engine before wiring infrastructure that hides policy bugs.

**Why this matters.** Operators approve and release held mail in a UI. Untyped form state is where “allow” vs “hold” bugs hide; **TypeScript** makes illegal states harder to represent, and **Vue 3** is how Module 08 structures that admin SPA. **How it works.** **Node.js** runs the toolchain (`npm`). TypeScript compiles typed `.ts` to JavaScript. Vue binds reactive state to templates so a hold-queue table updates when the API returns new rows. On the job, the same stack backs many SaaS security admin consoles: typed forms, clear dangerous actions, no cloud secrets in the browser bundle.

- **Node.js** — JavaScript runtime + npm for frontend tooling
- **TypeScript** — JavaScript with types

|---------|----------------|

# Go primer

**Why this matters.** Module 09’s worker consumes queue messages and applies hold/allow/reject. **Go** fits small, explicit network services: fast compile, static binaries, and straightforward concurrency — useful when a Python API owns HTTP and a worker owns async decisions. You *could* keep everything in one Python process; splitting a worker is how teams isolate retries, DLQs, and deploy cadence without blocking the API.

# Reading — Queue consumer + DLQ

## Learning objectives

1. Consume work from a queue behind an interface (LocalStack SQS in lab).
2. Make processing idempotent; route poison messages to a **dead-letter queue**.
3. Share a JSON contract with the API module.

**Why this matters.** Poison messages that never succeed will retry forever without a **dead-letter queue (DLQ)** — burning compute and blocking the main queue’s visibility window. Handlers that are not idempotent double-send mail on redelivery after a crash. Field drift between API JSON and Go structs causes silent parse failures in production. DLQs exist so humans can inspect failures without losing the original payload.

**How it works.** A consumer receives a message, processes it, then deletes it. If processing fails, the message becomes visible again (**at-least-once**). After `maxReceiveCount` / max attempts, the broker moves it to a DLQ. Your kata’s `ShouldDLQ(attempt, maxAttempts)` encodes that threshold (typically `attempt >= maxAttempts`). Idempotency keys (message id / hold id) prevent double side effects. Parse shared JSON carefully — same fields as Module 07.

```
Main queue → worker
   │ fail / redeliver (attempt++)
   └─ attempt >= max → DLQ (inspect, fix, replay)
```

**On the job.** SQS-style DLQs are standard in cloud mail and identity pipelines. Knowing when to DLQ vs retry — and how LocalStack demos the same shape — is day-to-day platform security engineering, not a single-vendor trick.

## Short intro

Queue consumers must survive crashes and bad payloads. Idempotency plus a DLQ turns “retry forever” into “park and investigate.”

# Reading — File / cloud-share DLP

## Learning objectives

1. Explain why **email hold** alone does not cover files shared via cloud links.
2. List controls: link visibility (org / specific users / public), expiry, app-level revoke, download audit. Note: a raw S3 **presigned URL** cannot be revoked individually — it stays valid until expiry (or until signing credentials / object policy are revoked). Real share-DLP revoke needs app-level indirection.
3. Relate Secure Drop’s expiring link to a minimal share-DLP story.

**Why this matters.** Outbound email hold catches messages on the mail path; it does nothing when someone pastes an “anyone with the link” URL into chat. Without visibility limits, expiry, revoke, and download audit, missent shares stay reachable until someone notices. Presigned URLs feel like revoke-able magic — until you learn a raw S3 presign is a **bearer** link that cannot be killed one-by-one. That trade-off is why production share-DLP puts an app check in front of short-lived presigns.

**How it works.** A share object records owner, visibility, `expires_at`, optional `revoked_at`, and audit events. Download flow: client hits **your** app → check not expired/revoked + authorized → issue a **short-lived** storage URL (or stream) → log who/when/object id (not file bytes). Email hold and share-DLP are complementary: hold is about SMTP content; share-DLP is about object links after the fact.

```
Upload → ShareLink (visibility, expiry, revoked_at)
Download → app authz check → short-lived fetch → audit metadata
Missend → set revoked_at → further downloads fail
```

**On the job.** Cloud Drive/SharePoint/S3-backed secure transfer shows up in every email and collaboration security review. Explaining why email DLP ≠ link DLP — and why revoke needs indirection — is vendor-neutral literacy for SaaS and cloud security roles.

## Short intro

Outbound email DLP catches messages and attachments on the mail path. People also paste cloud-share URLs into chat or leave “anyone with the link” open. File / cloud-share DLP is about **governing those shares**: who can open them, for how long, and what the audit log shows when someone downloads.

# Reading — Insecure password-ZIP transfer → Secure Drop

## Learning objectives

1. Explain the **global** insecure pattern: password-protected archive in one message, password in another on the **same channel**.
2. Why it fails: same-channel secrecy, blocks malware scanning, abused by malware loaders historically.
3. Prefer portal-style secure transfer: link + **recipient OTP**, expiry, and **revoke-after-missend**.

**Why this matters.** Sending a passworded ZIP and the password on the **same email channel** looks like encryption theater: anyone who compromised the mailbox gets both. Gateways cannot malware-scan encrypted archives, which is why loaders historically abused the pattern. Some regions nicknamed it “PPAP”; treat it as a **worldwide** anti-pattern, not a culture lesson. Secure Drop-style delivery exists because expiry, recipient proof, and **revoke-after-missend** beat hoping the wrong recipient deletes a ZIP.

**How it works.** Upload the file to object storage; create a share with expiry and a **hashed** recipient OTP (compare with a constant-time helper such as `hmac.compare_digest`). Recipient proves possession of OTP → short-lived download. On missend, operator **revokes** immediately so the link fails even if the URL was copied. Prefer this over same-channel ZIP+password; S/MIME or portal encryption may fit when you need end-to-end crypto with different threat models.

```
Sender uploads → Secure Drop link + OTP challenge
Recipient OTP OK → download → audit
Missend → revoke → further downloads fail
```

**On the job.** Secure file transfer and email DLP reviews always ask: can you revoke after missend, and can scanners see content? Answering with portal+OTP+revoke (and knowing ZIP+password fails) is core email/cloud security literacy.

## Short intro

Some regions nicknamed this pattern “PPAP”; treat it as a **worldwide** anti-pattern, not a culture lesson. Secure Drop-style delivery converts attachments to expiring download URLs with verification and revocation.

## Read these (verified)

1. [IIJ — PPAP report (English)](https://www.iij.ad.jp/en/dev/iir/pdf/iir_vol51_report_EN.pdf) — historical context
2. Module Secure Drop reading + object-storage [presigned URL docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html) for mechanism limits

# Reading — CI + cloud deploy

## Learning objectives

1. Run tests (and optionally build an image) on every PR/push.
2. Prefer federated OIDC roles over long-lived cloud keys in git.
3. Document a deploy path a stranger can follow.

**Why this matters.** Without Continuous Integration (**CI**), broken hold/allow rules and dependency regressions land on `main` and only surface in a demo or production. Long-lived cloud access keys in git (or even in Actions secrets) are a classic incident source: history, forks, and logs leak them, and rotation is slow. On the job, email and identity SaaS teams treat PR CI plus short-lived deploy credentials as table stakes — not optional polish.

**How it works.** A workflow YAML under `.github/workflows/` declares **when** to run (`on: push` / `pull_request`), **jobs** on runners, and **steps** (checkout → language setup → install → test). Optionally a later job builds a container image. Deploy (if any) should exchange an OpenID Connect (**OIDC**) token for a cloud role instead of storing `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` / secret keys. The kata checks workflow hygiene: forbidden secret-like patterns and a required test job name.

```text
PR/push → runner checkout → install deps → pytest/lint
                ↓ (optional)
         OIDC assume-role → push image / update service
```

## Short intro

Continuous Integration catches broken rules engines before merge. Cloud deploy should use short-lived credentials — GitHub Actions OIDC to a cloud role is the modern default. This module’s kata validates workflow hygiene helpers (detect forbidden secret patterns; require a test job name).

## Mechanism sketch (annotated)

Copy ideas from [`../starter/ci-sample.yml`](../starter/ci-sample.yml) into a workflow you own — never commit live secrets.

```yaml
# Why path filters: skip unrelated modules so CI stays fast and cheap
on:
  pull_request:
    paths: ["07-mailguard-api/**"]
jobs:
  unit-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4   # Why: runner starts empty; need the PR tree
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"    # Why: match the course Python pin
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt  # Why: reproducible deps before tests
      - run: pytest -q              # Why: contract must fail on stubs / broken rules
```

Prefer pinning third-party Actions by commit SHA in production (supply-chain hardening) — see OWASP CI/CD Security Top 10.

2. [GitHub Actions — OIDC with cloud providers](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/deployment/security-hardening-your-deployments/about-security-hardening-with-openid-connect)

# Reading — OIDC to AWS + ECS

## Learning objectives

1. Prefer **GitHub Actions OIDC** over long-lived `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` secrets.
2. Constrain role trust by `sub` (repo + ref).
3. Sketch an ECS Fargate deploy from CI.

**Why this matters.** Static AWS keys in repository secrets still leak via mis-logged env dumps, overly broad `permissions:`, and compromised maintainers. Federation with OpenID Connect (**OIDC**) issues **short-lived** credentials only when a trusted workflow runs. Without a tight trust policy (`sub` = this repo + `main`), any branch or fork workflow that can request the token becomes a cloud admin path. On the job, cloud-security reviews almost always ask how CI authenticates to the account that runs gateways, queues, and mail workers.

**How it works.**

1. Register GitHub’s OIDC issuer (`token.actions.githubusercontent.com`) as an Identity and Access Management (**IAM**) OIDC provider in AWS.
2. Create an IAM role whose trust policy allows `sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` only when JWT claims match (commonly `sub` like `repo:ORG/REPO:ref:refs/heads/main`).
3. In Actions, request an ID token, call AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity (often via `aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials`), then push an image and update **Amazon Elastic Container Service (ECS)** on **Fargate** (serverless tasks — no EC2 capacity management for the task itself).
4. Task definition pins image digest/tag, CPU/memory, and task role (least privilege to queues/buckets — not `AdministratorAccess`).

```text
GitHub job → OIDC JWT → AWS STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity
       → short-lived keys → ECR push / ECS service update
```

Trade-off vs long-lived keys: slightly more IAM/OIDC setup up front; far less key-rotation and leak blast radius. Trade-off vs “deploy from a laptop”: CI is auditable and repeatable; laptop tokens are not.

## Read these (verified)

1. [GitHub Actions — OIDC with AWS](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/deployment/security-hardening-your-deployments/configuring-openid-connect-in-amazon-web-services)
2. [AWS ECS on Fargate](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/AWS_Fargate.html)
3. [Terraform AWS provider — IAM OIDC](https://registry.terraform.io/providers/hashicorp/aws/latest/docs/resources/iam_openid_connect_provider)

## Starter sketch (do not apply blindly)

See [`../starter/oidc-aws-ecs.tf.example`](../starter/oidc-aws-ecs.tf.example). Why Terraform here: the trust condition and role are reviewable diffs — console clicks drift. Why constrain `sub`: so a feature-branch job cannot assume the production deploy role.

## On the job

Mail/identity services often land on ECS/Kubernetes behind CI. Interview and incident questions converge on the same mechanism: **who can assume the deploy role, from which repo/ref, and what can that role do afterward?**

## Next step

`oidc_aws` kata + starter Terraform sketch → quiz.

# Terraform / HCL primer

**Why this matters.** Clicking a cloud console does not review well and drifts silently. **Terraform** expresses buckets, IAM, and queues as code so Module 13 can `plan` changes before they hit a real account. On the job, reviewers read the plan — not a console screenshot — when mail/identity infra changes.

**How it works.** You write **HCL** (HashiCorp Configuration Language) describing desired resources. `terraform plan` shows a diff; `apply` mutates cloud APIs; **state** maps real IDs back to your config — and must not be committed when it contains secrets.

This primer has no assignment, quiz, or download pack.

---

## What Terraform is

**Terraform** is an infrastructure-as-code tool. Config files commonly use the `.tf` extension and HCL syntax.

## Why industry uses it

Reviewable infra diffs, repeatable environments, and clearer least-privilege IAM stories. Security reviews often start from the plan output, not from a console screenshot.

## Key concepts for Module 13

| Concept | Why you care |
|---------|----------------|
| Providers | Talk to AWS (or others) via APIs |
| Resources | Bucket, queue, IAM policy blocks |
| `plan` vs `apply` | See blast radius before change |
| Remote state (awareness) | Team sharing without git-stored secrets |

## Install and run

1. [Terraform install](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/install)
2. Check: `terraform version`

You do not need cloud credentials for this primer — Module 13 documents plan against *your* resources or local stand-ins.

## Tiny hands-on example

```hcl
# Conceptual — do not apply without credentials and a backend you own
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.5"
}

# Why: a local_file resource proves HCL parses without a cloud account
resource "local_file" "primer" {
  filename = "${path.module}/primer-note.txt"
  content  = "mailguard terraform primer\n"
}
```

```bash
mkdir -p /tmp/mg-tf-primer && cd /tmp/mg-tf-primer
# Why /tmp: keep the primer throwaway; do not mix with real state
# paste the HCL into main.tf, then:
terraform init   # Why: download providers declared in the config
terraform plan   # Why: see the diff before any apply
```

**How:** `init` installs providers; `plan` shows it would create a local file — same discipline as planning IAM/bucket changes later.

## Official docs

1. [Terraform intro](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/intro)
2. [Terraform install](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/install)
3. [HCL language resources](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language)

# Reading — Cloud IAM & misconfiguration posture

## Learning objectives

1. Explain Identity and Access Management (**IAM**) as identities + permissions + resources.
2. Apply a least-privilege review to a MailGuard bucket/queue role.
3. Describe shared responsibility at a high level (provider secures cloud; you secure *in* cloud).

**Why this matters.** Broken cloud IAM — public storage, wildcard `*` actions, root-like keys in CI — causes real incidents more often than exotic crypto bugs. Hold queues, Secure Drop objects, and worker roles all inherit whatever permissions you grant. Without a posture checklist, Terraform/`apply` can look “green” while leaving world-readable buckets or admin-equivalent runtime roles. On the job, cloud-security and identity teams review IAM before they review application code.

**How it works.** IAM binds **principals** (users, roles, services) to **actions** on **resources** via policies. Least privilege means the MailGuard API/worker role can read/write only the buckets and queues it needs — not `s3:*` / `iam:*` on `*`. Shared responsibility: the provider secures the platform (datacenters, hypervisor, managed control planes); you secure accounts, identities, network exposure, encryption choices, and data *in* the cloud. Module 13 Terraform/Compose (and the Module 12 CI deploy identity) are where you practice that review — National Institute of Standards and Technology (**NIST**) vocabulary welcome; no cert wall.

```text
Identity (role) → Policy (Allow/Deny actions) → Resource (bucket/queue)
                      ↑
              CI OIDC / app runtime assumes this role
```

Trade-offs: broad roles ship features faster and explode blast radius; narrow roles need more planning when new queues appear. Prefer plan-time checks over “we’ll tighten later.”

## Short intro

This reading prepares a checklist you will run against your Module 13 Terraform/Compose (and the Module 12 CI deploy identity).

## Videos (verified)

1. Prefer [AWS IAM User Guide — Introduction](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/introduction.html) first (authoritative). Optional video: search freeCodeCamp / AWS “IAM explained” and confirm the current title before watching.  
   Why it helps: users/roles/policies mental model.

2. Optional: search “cloud misconfiguration public S3” conference talks for incident stories — treat as case studies, not product ads.

Prefer official IAM docs below if videos move.

## Annotated posture moves

| Check | Why that way |
|-------|----------------|
| No long-lived keys in git | History/forks leak; prefer OIDC / short-lived creds |
| Bucket Block Public Access on | Default-deny stops accidental `Principal: "*"` exposure |
| Runtime role ≠ admin | Compromise of the API process should not rewrite IAM |
| Secrets in a store / env, not state jokes | Terraform state can contain sensitive values — lock down remote state |

Example mindset for a lab-only misconfig: turn Block Public Access off and add a public bucket policy — then detect with `terraform plan`, a policy scanner, or a Scout/Prowler-class tool, and remediate. Why intentionally break a *lab* bucket: muscle memory for detection before production.

## Read these (verified)

1. [AWS IAM — User guide (roles & policies)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/introduction.html) — core model.
2. [AWS — Security best practices in IAM](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/best-practices.html)
3. [CIS Amazon Web Services Foundations Benchmark](https://www.cisecurity.org/benchmark/amazon_web_services) — awareness of common hardened baselines (download may require form; skim public summaries OK).
4. [NIST CSF overview](https://www.nist.gov/cyberframework) — identify/protect framing without exam prep.
5. [OWASP — Cloud Native Application Security Top 10](https://owasp.org/projects/cloud-native-application-security-top-10) — cloud-native risks adjacent to IAM/misconfig posture (also see [CI/CD Security Top 10](https://owasp.org/www-project-top-10-ci-cd-security-risks/)).

# Kubernetes YAML primer

**Why this matters.** Compose is enough for a laptop story; **Kubernetes** is how many teams run the same containers with health probes, restarts, and resource requests. Module 14 puts MailGuard’s shape on kind/minikube before GitOps in Module 16. On the job, API/worker pods for mail and identity services live here — probes and requests are the difference between a quiet restart and a silent outage.

**How it works.** You declare desired state in **YAML** (Deployment, Service, etc.). The control plane reconciles actual pods toward that state. **kubectl** is the CLI; **kind**/**minikube** give you a local cluster without a cloud bill.

This primer has no assignment, quiz, or download pack.

---

## What Kubernetes YAML is

**Kubernetes** schedules containers across nodes. You rarely “SSH and start a process” — you apply manifests that describe replicas, probes, and networking.

## Why industry uses it

Self-healing workloads, consistent deploy APIs across clouds, and a clear path to policy/GitOps. Security teams care about resource limits, probes, and later NetworkPolicy/admission controls.

## Key concepts for Module 14

| Concept | Why you care |
|---------|----------------|
| Pod | Smallest runnable unit (usually one app container) |
| Deployment | Keeps N replicas; rolling updates |
| Service | Stable networking to pods |
| Probes / requests | Readiness and CPU/memory — Module 14 requires these |

## Install and run

1. [kubectl install](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/tools/)
2. Cluster tools wait for Module 14: [kind](https://kind.sigs.k8s.io/docs/user/quick-start/) or [minikube](https://minikube.sigs.k8s.io/docs/start/)

**Check now:** `kubectl version --client`  
Why `--client` only: confirm the CLI is installed without needing a cluster API yet (Module 14 starts the cluster).

## Tiny hands-on example

```yaml
# Conceptual snippet — apply only inside Module 14's cluster
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: mailguard-api
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: mailguard-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: mailguard-api
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: example/mailguard-api:primer
          # Why: probes come next in Module 14 — without them traffic may hit a dead process
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
```

**How:** The Deployment names a Pod template; Kubernetes creates pods matching the selector — Module 14 adds probes and resource requests on top of this shape.

## Official docs

1. [Kubernetes overview](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/)
2. [Deployments](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/)
3. [kubectl cheat sheet](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/kubectl/cheatsheet/)

---

## Done when

You can explain **why** this tool shows up on the MailGuard path and **how** to install/run the tiny example. Mark this primer complete on the site, then continue to the next module (`14-k8s-local`).

This primer has **no** assignment, quiz, or download pack.

## Learning objectives

1. Run the app on kind/minikube with probes and requests.
2. Prefer Helm or Kustomize overlays for env differences.
3. Name managed Kubernetes + GitOps as the production next step.

**Why this matters.** Copy-pasting raw YAML per environment (dev/stage/prod) drifts: one cluster gets probes, another does not. **Helm** charts and **Kustomize** overlays keep a shared base and patch only what must change (replicas, image tag, ingress host). Without that discipline, “works on kind” silently differs from “what we shipped.” On the job, platform teams expect env overlays — and then GitOps (Module 16) to sync them.

**How it works.** Base manifests describe Deployment/Service/probes. Kustomize `kustomization.yaml` lists resources + patches; Helm templates values (`values.yaml`) into charts. You render or install into the local cluster, still verifying Ready pods. Managed Kubernetes (EKS/GKE/AKS-class) later replaces the DIY control plane; a pull agent (Argo CD-class) replaces laptop `kubectl apply`.

```text
base YAML → Helm values / Kustomize overlay → rendered manifests → cluster
```

Trade-off: raw YAML is easiest to read for one file; overlays scale when env diffs grow. Prefer overlays over forked copies.

## Annotated commands

```bash
# Why render before install: catch template errors without mutating the cluster
helm template myapp ./chart -f values-dev.yaml | kubectl apply -f -

# Or Kustomize:
kubectl apply -k overlays/dev   # Why -k: build overlay then apply in one step
```

# Reading — K8s local

## Learning objectives

1. Run a Deployment + Service on kind or minikube.
2. Add liveness/readiness probes and CPU/memory requests.
3. Know what you have not automated yet (GitOps, policy).

**Why this matters.** A container that “runs on my laptop” is not enough for a mail/identity API: processes die, dependencies hang, and noisy neighbors steal memory. Without readiness probes, Services send traffic to pods that are not ready; without resource requests, the scheduler cannot place work fairly and a leak can OOM-kill neighbors. On the job, platform and security reviews ask for probes, requests/limits, and an honest gap list (no GitOps yet, no NetworkPolicy yet) before calling a chart “production-shaped.”

**How it works.** You create a local cluster (**kind** or **minikube**), apply YAML for a **Deployment** (Pod template + replica controller) and a **Service** (stable virtual IP/DNS to matching pods). The kubelet runs **probes**: readiness gates Service endpoints; liveness triggers restarts of stuck processes. **Requests** tell the scheduler how much CPU/memory the pod needs. You are not yet doing pull-based GitOps or admission policy — Module 16 covers that.

```text
kubectl apply → API server → controllers create Pods
Pods pass readiness → Endpoints populate → Service routes traffic
liveness fail → kubelet restarts container
```

## Short intro

Containers need orchestration for restarts, probes, and resource requests. Start local (kind/minikube), keep manifests small, and document gaps honestly.

## Annotated local loop

```bash
# Why kind/minikube: practice the API without a cloud bill
kind create cluster   # or: minikube start

# Why apply Deployment+Service together: pods without a Service are hard to reach stably
kubectl apply -f starter/deployment.yaml

# Why get pods: confirm Ready before claiming the demo works
kubectl get pods
```

In the Deployment, set readiness/liveness HTTP paths and `resources.requests` — why: Module 14’s checks expect them; production reviewers will too. Prefer a pinned image tag over `:latest` so restarts are reproducible.

## Read these (verified)

1. [Kubernetes — Deployments](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/)
2. [Configure Liveness, Readiness and Startup Probes](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-liveness-readiness-startup-probes/)
3. [kind — Quick Start](https://kind.sigs.k8s.io/docs/user/quick-start/)
4. [Resource requests and limits](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/manage-resources-containers/)

## On the job

Email gateways and identity sidecars often run as Deployments. Knowing **how** probes and requests behave under failure is more valuable than memorizing every kubectl flag.

Continue with the assignment from the downloads on this page.

# Reading — Incident response & detection

## Learning objectives

1. Apply **NIST SP 800-61r3** lifecycle language to MailGuard incidents.
2. Triage identity alerts (e.g. impossible travel) at a conceptual level.
3. Write a **blameless English postmortem** (impact, timeline, actions) — no secondary-language summary line required.

**Why this matters.** Hold-queue privacy incidents, missend+revoke events, and admin “impossible travel” alerts do not wait for a perfect runbook. Without a shared lifecycle vocabulary, teams skip preparation, thrash during containment, and write blame-heavy writeups that do not prevent recurrence. On the job, email and identity security teams are expected to triage signals quickly, contain access, and document impact in clear English for legal/privacy partners.

**How it works.** National Institute of Standards and Technology (**NIST**) SP 800-61r3 frames incident response as a lifecycle (preparation → detection/analysis → containment/eradication/recovery → post-incident activity). For MailGuard-shaped events:

1. **Preparation** — logging, roles, contacts, SLIs that show hold/release health.
2. **Detection** — alert on anomalous admin sign-in (e.g. impossible travel) or sudden hold-queue access.
3. **Containment** — revoke sessions/keys, freeze risky releases, limit who can read held content.
4. **Post-incident** — blameless postmortem with impact, timeline, root causes (tech + process), and owners for actions.

```text
Signal → triage (false positive?) → contain access → eradicate cause
      → recover service → postmortem + detection improvements
```

Trade-off: aggressive auto-lockouts reduce attacker dwell time but can lock out legitimate travelers — document human review paths. Keep Endpoint Detection and Response (**EDR**) / Managed Detection and Response (**MDR**) discussion vendor-neutral.

## Keep in mind

EDR/MDR are concepts here — stay vendor-neutral. Detection content is English-only for course artifacts.

## Read these (verified)

1. [NIST SP 800-61r3](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/61/r3/final)
2. Existing module SRE / golden signals reading
3. Cloud identity sign-in log docs for the IdP you use in lab

## On the job

Interview and IR drills ask for **how** you decide severity and **why** you notify privacy/security stakeholders when held mail may contain personal data — not just which button you clicked in a vendor console.
