# Reading — SRE basics (SLI / SLO / error budgets / postmortem)

## Learning objectives

1. Define **SLI**, **SLO**, and **error budget** and relate them to MailGuard’s hold pipeline.
2. Prefer user-visible indicators (e.g. successful release within N seconds) over vanity metrics.
3. Write a short **blameless postmortem** from telemetry.

**Why this matters.** Observability without objectives becomes dashboard tourism: lots of charts, no decision rule. When hold enqueue or release latency silently degrades, operators and users notice before vanity counters do. Site Reliability Engineering (**SRE**) popularized measuring reliability with Service Level Indicators (**SLI**s), targeting them with Service Level Objectives (**SLO**s), and spending **error budgets** when reality misses the target — then learning via postmortems. On the job, email/identity on-call uses those budgets to choose “ship features” vs “freeze and harden.”

**How it works.**

1. Pick user-visible **SLIs** (e.g. fraction of release API calls completing in < 30s; hold-enqueue success rate).
2. Set an **SLO** over a window (e.g. 99% over 28 days).
3. The **error budget** is the allowed failure fraction (here ~1%). Burn it → pause risky launches; recover budget → resume feature work.
4. Emit signals (metrics/traces/logs via OpenTelemetry-class tooling) so you can prove burn and write a **blameless** postmortem (systems/process fixes, not blame).

```text
User journey → SLI events (good/bad) → SLO compliance → error budget left?
                                                      ↓ burned
                                            reliability work / freeze
```

Trade-off: tight SLOs create more freezes; loose SLOs hide user pain. Prefer fewer meaningful SLIs over dozens of vanity gauges.

## Short intro

SRE vocabulary turns telemetry into release policy — not just pretty graphs.

## Videos (verified)

1. **[SLIs, SLOs, SLAs, oh my! (class SRE implements DevOps)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tEylFyxbDLE)** — Google Cloud Tech  
   Why it helps: canonical vocabulary with examples.

2. **[Risk and Error Budgets (class SRE implements DevOps)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=y2ILKr8kCJU)** — Google Cloud Tech  
   Why it helps: how error budgets drive release vs reliability trade-offs; pair with written postmortem culture chapter.

Prefer the Google SRE book chapters below if a video moves.

## Annotated practice

When you wire metrics later:

```text
# Why count good/bad release events — not “CPU looks fine”:
# decisions need user-visible success criteria
release_success{le="30s"} / release_attempts
```

Alert on **burn rate over a window**, not every single failure — why: avoid pager fatigue that trains people to ignore real incidents.

## Read these (verified)

1. [Google SRE Book — Service Level Objectives](https://sre.google/sre-book/service-level-objectives/) — SLI/SLO/error budgets.
2. [Google SRE Book — Postmortem Culture](https://sre.google/sre-book/postmortem-culture/) — blameless learning.
3. [OpenTelemetry docs — Concepts](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/) — signals you will emit in this module.
4. [Google — CRE life lessons / SLOs](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/gcp/sre-fundamentals-slis-slas-and-slos) — short companion.

# Reading — Argo CD, policy-as-code, Crossplane intro

## Learning objectives

1. Explain **pull** GitOps (Argo CD app-of-apps) vs push pipelines.
2. Fail CI on bad manifests with Kyverno or Conftest.
3. Sketch a Crossplane claim for cloud resources (generic intro).

**Why this matters.** As services multiply (API, worker, admin UI), one flat folder of manifests becomes unreviewable. **App-of-apps** patterns let a root Application own child apps so each team’s repo/path stays clear. Without policy, privileged pods or missing probes still sync “successfully.” **Crossplane** (awareness-level here) brings cloud resources into the same Kubernetes control loop via claims — useful when identity/mail infra should be requested like any other API object. On the job, platform interviews often contrast pull vs push and ask how bad YAML is blocked.

**How it works.**

1. **Argo CD** (pull): controller compares live state to git; syncs when drifted.
2. **App-of-apps**: root Application manifests point at child Applications (API, worker, …).
3. **Policy-as-code**: Conftest/Kyverno reject privileged pods, `:latest`, missing probes in CI or admission.
4. **Crossplane claim**: a namespaced custom resource requests composed cloud infra (bucket/queue) without every app team learning raw cloud consoles — Terraform remains valid; Crossplane is another composition style.

```text
Root App → Child App (api) → Deployment/Service in git
         → Child App (worker)
CI: conftest/kyverno on PR  →  Argo sync only green desired state
```

# Reading — GitOps + policy

## Learning objectives

1. Diagram pull-based sync of manifests from git.
2. Fail CI on a policy violation (e.g. missing probes).
3. Keep claims proportional to what you automated.

**Why this matters.** Laptop `kubectl apply` does not scale and is hard to audit. Drift appears when someone “just fixed prod” outside git. Policy-as-code stops unsafe desired state (no probes, `:latest`, privileged pods) before it becomes the cluster’s reality. On the job, platform and security teams expect git as the source of truth for what runs mail/identity workloads — and CI gates that reject bad manifests.

**How it works.** GitOps treats git as the desired state; a sync agent applies it. In **pull** mode, an in-cluster agent (Argo CD-class) watches the repo and reconciles. In **push** mode, CI runs `kubectl`/`helm` from outside. Policy tools (Kyverno, OPA/Gatekeeper, Conftest) validate manifests in CI or at admission. This module reuses Module 14 checks and adds a “bad manifest” fixture that must fail.

```text
git commit (desired) → CI policy check → sync agent pulls → cluster matches git
                              ↓ fail
                         PR blocked (bad probes/tags/privileges)
```

Trade-off: pull GitOps needs an agent and RBAC in-cluster; push is simpler to start but credentials live in CI and drift is easier if people apply by hand.

## Short intro

GitOps + policy-as-code turn “hope the YAML is safe” into enforceable gates.

## Annotated checks

```bash
# Why fail CI before sync: stop bad desired-state from rolling out
conftest test fixtures/bad_deployment.yaml -p policy/
# or Kyverno/OPA equivalent — same idea: deny missing probes / privileged pods
```

Keep claims honest: if you only failed a fixture in CI, do not say “production GitOps” yet.

## Learning objectives

1. Build a small awareness quiz UI (Svelte preferred).
2. Label the experience as a learning simulation.
3. Prefer report-rate metrics over “gotcha” humiliation.

**Why this matters.** Phishing remains a top initial-access path into mail and identity systems. # Reading — OSS contribution & security UX

## Learning objectives

1. Describe a respectful OSS contribution loop (read contributing guide → issue → minimal PR → respond to review).
2. List three qualities of a good **security warning** in an admin UI (clarity, action, no alarm fatigue).
3. Explain why phishing *simulations* need consent/honesty framing when used for learning.

**Why this matters.** Solo repos do not prove you can collaborate on security-sensitive code. Weak warning UX (scary modals users click through forever) creates alarm fatigue and missends still ship. Career-prep portfolios that show “I can collaborate beyond a solo repo” often include a small upstream contribution and evidence you care how humans meet security controls. On the job, mail/identity admin UIs live or die on clear hold/release warnings — not denser red banners.

**How it works.**

1. **OSS loop:** read `CONTRIBUTING` → find/create issue → minimal PR with test plan → respond to review.
2. **Security UX:** state the risk, the consequence, and the primary/secondary actions; avoid permanent one-click dismiss of critical warnings.
3. **Training honesty:** learning UIs disclose purpose; never harvest credentials (ties to Module 17).

```text
Read guide → reproduce → small PR → CI + review → merge
Hold UI: clear consequence → confirm release → audit log
```

Trade-off: more friction on release can prevent missend but slows legitimate ops — design confirmations that match severity.

MailGuard’s admin hold/release flow is a natural place to practice warning copy and confirmation UX.

# Capstone — small mail filter end-to-end

This module closes the course: ship a **coherent demo** of outbound message filtering (hold / allow / reject), prove it with tests, and self-grade against [`../../CAPSTONE-RUBRIC.md`](../../CAPSTONE-RUBRIC.md).

**Why this matters.** Separate labs (rules, API, worker, CI, IAM) do not prove you can tell one story. Hiring managers and portfolio reviewers look for a runnable thread: sample messages in → policy actions out → tests green → honest gaps. Without that integration, skills look like disconnected checklists. On the job, outbound missend prevention is exactly this shape — ordered rules, operator release path, and evidence you did not hard-code secrets.

**How it works.**

1. Define an ordered **rule list** (first-match-wins unless you document another order).
2. Actions: `hold`, `allow`, `reject` on sample fixtures (internal/external, risky recipients, keywords).
3. Prove behavior with **table-driven tests** that fail on empty stubs — why: green stubs would not prove your code.
4. Show an **operator path** (print held queue or approve/release helper).

A stranger can:

1. Read your short demo notes

# Reading — SCIM / JIT / directories

## Learning objectives

1. Describe SCIM 2.0 resources and filtering (RFC 7643/7644).
2. Contrast JIT vs SCIM vs directory sync (e.g. Entra Connect patterns).
3. Explain why **deprovisioning latency** often matters more than provisioning speed.

**Why this matters.** Joiner speed feels like a helpdesk win; **leaver lag** is a security incident waiting to happen — ex-employees who still reach hold queues, admin consoles, or mailbox forwards. System for Cross-domain Identity Management (**SCIM**) 2.0 standardizes create/update/deactivate across SaaS apps. Just-In-Time (**JIT**) provisioning creates users on first single sign-on (**SSO**) but may not tear them down promptly. On the job, identity engineers are measured on deprovision SLAs as much as onboarding UX.

**How it works.**

1. **RFC 7643** defines resources (User, Group) and schemas; **RFC 7644** defines the HTTP protocol (`/Users`, filters, PATCH).
2. An Identity Provider (**IdP**) (or broker) POSTs/PATCHes users into the app’s SCIM endpoint; clients often **filter** first (`userName eq …`) to avoid duplicates.
3. **JIT:** account appears at first SSO — simple, but lifecycle depends on later hooks.
4. **Directory sync** (e.g. Entra Connect-class): continuous sync from on-prem/cloud directories — different operational model than app-level SCIM.
5. Deprovision: disable login **and** revoke app roles, tokens, forwarding, and group grants — incomplete disable leaves access paths.

```text
IdP lifecycle event → SCIM POST/PATCH/DELETE → app account state
                 ↘ JIT on first SSO (create only unless hooked)
```

Trade-off: SCIM needs a correct endpoint and filter support; JIT is faster to ship and weaker on leavers unless you add lifecycle jobs.

## Lab idea

Minimal FastAPI SCIM `/Users` endpoint passing a subset of filters; optionally validate against a vendor SCIM test harness.

```text
# Why support filter: IdPs query before create/update
GET /Users?filter=userName eq "ada@example.com"
```

## Read these (verified)

1. [RFC 7643 — SCIM core](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7643)
2. [RFC 7644 — SCIM protocol](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7644)
3. [Microsoft Entra — SCIM overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/app-provisioning/use-scim-to-provision-users-and-groups)
4. [Google Workspace — Admin SDK Directory API](https://developers.google.com/admin-sdk/directory)

## On the job

Mail-security products inherit every account the IdP still believes is active. Ask “what happens at T+24h after termination?” before celebrating join latency.

## Next step

Assignments → katas → quiz.

# Reading — Global collaboration & privacy

## Learning objectives

1. Collaborate across timezones: async updates, explicit handoffs, inclusive meeting hygiene.
2. Compare major privacy laws at a literacy level: **GDPR**, **CCPA/CPRA**, **APPI**, **LGPD**, **PIPL**.
3. Connect privacy duties to MailGuard hold/release (minimization, access, retention, cross-border caution).

**Why this matters.** Hold queues can contain personal data (message bodies, recipients, attachments). A support engineer in another country asking for “just paste the held mail” can create a cross-border transfer problem. Global teams that only schedule meetings at one region’s afternoon quietly exclude others and slow incident response. On the job, email/identity SaaS work is multi-region by default — privacy literacy and async handoffs are operational skills, not soft extras.

**How it works.**

1. **Collaboration:** prefer written async handoffs with timezone stamps; rotate meeting hours or default to async; explicit owner for the next action.
2. **Privacy literacy:** General Data Protection Regulation (**GDPR**), California Consumer Privacy Act / California Privacy Rights Act (**CCPA/CPRA**), Japan’s Act on the Protection of Personal Information (**APPI**), Brazil’s Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados (**LGPD**), China’s Personal Information Protection Law (**PIPL**) — different scopes and breach-notification expectations; cite primary sources, do not memorize every article.
3. **MailGuard link:** minimize what the hold store keeps, restrict who can release/read, define retention, and check transfer rules before foreign support access.

```text
Incident spanning TZ A/B → async handoff note → least-privilege access check
                         → privacy regime checklist → notify / refuse as needed
```

## Keep in mind

No language-learning drills. No employer-specific culture decks. Focus on professional norms that travel: clarity, respect for local holidays/time, and privacy-by-design.

## Read these (verified)

1. [GDPR.eu overview](https://gdpr.eu/) (prefer EUR-Lex for normative text)
2. [California CPPA — CCPA/CPRA](https://cppa.ca.gov/)
3. [Japan PPC English](https://www.ppc.go.jp/en/)
4. [Brazil ANPD (LGPD)](https://www.gov.br/anpd/pt-br)
5. Optional PIPL overview from reputable legal summaries — verify against official PRC texts when making compliance claims.

## On the job

Interview scenarios often ask: “Support overseas needs hold contents — what do you check first?” Lawful basis / transfer / least privilege / retention beats “sure, here’s the PDF.”

## Next step

Assignments → kata → quiz.

# Reading — Git & code review

## Learning objectives

1. Open small, reviewable PRs with clear English descriptions.
2. Review for security: secrets, authz, input validation, dangerous defaults.
3. Use conventional commits, CODEOWNERS, and CI logs effectively.
4. Write a one-page design note / RFC-style proposal.

**Why this matters.** Large mixed PRs hide auth bugs; vague commits block bisect; approving a PEM in `config/` creates a breach. MailGuard-shaped changes (hold/release, identity, CI) need reviewers who ask **why** and **how**, not only “LGTM.” On the job, collaboration skills are how secure changes land without silent regressions.

**How it works.**

1. Branch → small commits with [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/) subjects (`feat:`, `fix:`, `docs:` …).
2. Open a PR with intent, risk, and test plan; keep diff focused (split refactors from auth).
3. **CODEOWNERS** routes required reviewers by path.
4. Reviewers check secrets, authz, validation, dangerous defaults; CI logs triage red jobs before merge.
5. For larger ideas, write a one-page design/RFC before coding — why: align threat model and UX before sunk cost.

```text
idea → short RFC → small PR → CI → security-minded review → merge
```

Trade-off: tiny PRs add merge overhead but cut review risk; mega-PRs feel faster and ship hidden footguns.

## Annotated review habits

```bash
# Why conventional subject: changelog + bisect clarity
git commit -m "fix: require readinessProbe on api deployment"

# Why read CI logs before re-running blindly: find the failing contract fast
# Why block *.pem in PRs: secrets in git outlive the PR tab
```

entries.snippet: Browser API for phishing-resistant authenticators (security keys / passkeys).

entries.title: Passkey
entries.body: User-friendly WebAuthn credential (often synced or device-bound) for phishing-resistant sign-in.
entries.snippet: User-friendly WebAuthn credential (often synced or device-bound) for phishing-resistant sign-in.

entries.title: Identity Provider (IdP)
entries.body: Service that authenticates users and issues assertions/tokens to relying apps.
entries.snippet: Service that authenticates users and issues assertions/tokens to relying apps.

entries.title: ZTNA — Zero Trust Network Access
entries.body: App-scoped remote access that verifies identity (and often device context) instead of broad VPN LAN admission.
entries.snippet: App-scoped remote access that verifies identity (and often device context) instead of broad VPN LAN admission.

entries.title: VPN — Virtual Private Network
entries.body: Encrypted tunnel into a network; classical remote access often admits users to wide internal ranges.
entries.snippet: Encrypted tunnel into a network; classical remote access often admits users to wide internal ranges.

entries.title: Device certificate / posture
entries.body: Cryptographic device identity or health signals used as extra access context (conceptually; not a full MDM course).
entries.snippet: Cryptographic device identity or health signals used as extra access context (conceptually; not a full MDM course).

entries.title: DLP — Data Loss Prevention
entries.body: Policies that detect/block sensitive data leaving approved channels (e.g. email or cloud shares).
entries.snippet: Policies that detect/block sensitive data leaving approved channels (e.g. email or cloud shares).

entries.title: Missend
entries.body: Accidental delivery to the wrong recipient (typo, wrong autocomplete, mixed internal/external).
entries.snippet: Accidental delivery to the wrong recipient (typo, wrong autocomplete, mixed internal/external).

entries.title: BEC — Business Email Compromise
entries.body: Fraud that hijacks or spoofs business email to trick victims (e.g. fake payment requests).
entries.snippet: Fraud that hijacks or spoofs business email to trick victims (e.g. fake payment requests).

entries.title: SMTP — Simple Mail Transfer Protocol
entries.body: Store-and-forward protocol that moves email between servers (and submission clients).
entries.snippet: Store-and-forward protocol that moves email between servers (and submission clients).

entries.title: SPF — Sender Policy Framework

entries.title: DKIM — DomainKeys Identified Mail
entries.body: Cryptographic signature on email with a public key published in DNS.
entries.snippet: Cryptographic signature on email with a public key published in DNS.

entries.title: DMARC — Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance
entries.body: Policy + alignment of the visible From domain with SPF/DKIM results, plus reporting.
entries.snippet: Policy + alignment of the visible From domain with SPF/DKIM results, plus reporting.

entries.title: MX — Mail Exchanger
entries.body: DNS record type that names the hosts that accept mail for a domain.
entries.snippet: DNS record type that names the hosts that accept mail for a domain.

entries.title: Hold / suspend
entries.body: Temporary quarantine of a message pending review or timeout — neither allow nor hard reject.
entries.snippet: Temporary quarantine of a message pending review or timeout — neither allow nor hard reject.

entries.title: Allow / reject (discard)
entries.body: Policy actions: pass through vs block (and often drop) the message.
entries.snippet: Policy actions: pass through vs block (and often drop) the message.

entries.title: First-match-wins
entries.body: Evaluate ordered rules; stop at the first matching rule’s action.
entries.snippet: Evaluate ordered rules; stop at the first matching rule’s action.

entries.title: Secure transfer
entries.body: Controlled file sharing (upload, store, expiring link, audit) instead of raw email attachments.
entries.snippet: Controlled file sharing (upload, store, expiring link, audit) instead of raw email attachments.

entries.title: Cloud-share DLP
entries.body: Governing file links (visibility, expiry, revoke, audit) beyond the email path.
entries.snippet: Governing file links (visibility, expiry, revoke, audit) beyond the email path.

entries.title: Software as a Service (SaaS)
entries.body: Vendor-hosted software delivered over the network; MailGuard is a *learning* SaaS shape, not a product clone.
entries.snippet: Vendor-hosted software delivered over the network; MailGuard is a *learning* SaaS shape, not a product clone.

entries.title: TLS — Transport Layer Security
entries.body: Protocol that encrypts and authenticates network connections (e.g. HTTPS, SMTP with TLS).
entries.snippet: Protocol that encrypts and authenticates network connections (e.g. HTTPS, SMTP with TLS).

entries.title: X.509 certificate
entries.body: Signed binding of a public key to a name (and related fields), used in TLS trust chains.
entries.snippet: Signed binding of a public key to a name (and related fields), used in TLS trust chains.

entries.title: AEAD — Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data
entries.body: Encryption that also detects tampering; associated data is authenticated but not encrypted.
entries.snippet: Encryption that also detects tampering; associated data is authenticated but not encrypted.

entries.title: HMAC — Hash-based Message Authentication Code
entries.body: Keyed hash proving integrity/authenticity; also listed under Identity when used for OTP.
entries.snippet: Keyed hash proving integrity/authenticity; also listed under Identity when used for OTP.

entries.title: API — Application Programming Interface
entries.body: Contract for how clients talk to a service (here, often HTTP/JSON).
entries.snippet: Contract for how clients talk to a service (here, often HTTP/JSON).

entries.title: FastAPI
entries.body: Modern Python web framework for building APIs with type hints and OpenAPI docs.
entries.snippet: Modern Python web framework for building APIs with type hints and OpenAPI docs.

entries.title: OpenAPI
entries.body: Standard description of an HTTP API (formerly Swagger); used for docs and client generation.
entries.snippet: Standard description of an HTTP API (formerly Swagger); used for docs and client generation.

entries.title: CRUD — Create, Read, Update, Delete
entries.body: Basic resource operations on stored entities.
entries.snippet: Basic resource operations on stored entities.

entries.title: SPA — Single-Page Application
entries.body: Frontend that updates in-browser (e.g. Vue admin) talking to an API.
entries.snippet: Frontend that updates in-browser (e.g. Vue admin) talking to an API.

entries.title: E2E — End-to-End
entries.body: Test that drives the full user path (UI → API → storage), not just one unit.
entries.snippet: Test that drives the full user path (UI → API → storage), not just one unit.

entries.title: DLQ — Dead-Letter Queue
entries.body: Side queue for messages that failed processing after retries.
entries.snippet: Side queue for messages that failed processing after retries.

entries.title: AWS — Amazon Web Services
entries.body: Major public cloud; used here for deploy/storage/queue practice.
entries.snippet: Major public cloud; used here for deploy/storage/queue practice.

entries.title: Infrastructure as Code (IaC)
entries.body: Declare infra in files (e.g. Terraform) and apply via tooling, not click-ops alone.
entries.snippet: Declare infra in files (e.g. Terraform) and apply via tooling, not click-ops alone.

entries.title: IAM — Identity and Access Management
entries.body: Cloud users/roles/policies controlling who can do what on which resources.
entries.snippet: Cloud users/roles/policies controlling who can do what on which resources.

entries.title: CI — Continuous Integration
entries.body: Automated build/test (and often lint) on each change, typically via GitHub Actions here.
entries.snippet: Automated build/test (and often lint) on each change, typically via GitHub Actions here.

entries.title: SBOM — Software Bill of Materials
entries.body: Inventory of components/dependencies in an artifact for supply-chain review.
entries.snippet: Inventory of components/dependencies in an artifact for supply-chain review.

entries.title: Kubernetes (K8s)
entries.body: Container orchestration API; local practice via kind/minikube before managed clusters.
entries.snippet: Container orchestration API; local practice via kind/minikube before managed clusters.

entries.title: EKS — Elastic Kubernetes Service
entries.body: AWS-managed Kubernetes control plane (named as a *next step*, not required locally).
entries.snippet: AWS-managed Kubernetes control plane (named as a *next step*, not required locally).

entries.title: OpenTelemetry (OTel)
entries.body: Vendor-neutral APIs/SDKs for traces, metrics, and logs.
entries.snippet: Vendor-neutral APIs/SDKs for traces, metrics, and logs.

entries.title: SRE — Site Reliability Engineering
entries.body: Practice of running reliable systems with engineering + operations habits (SLIs/SLOs, postmortems).
entries.snippet: Practice of running reliable systems with engineering + operations habits (SLIs/SLOs, postmortems).

entries.title: SLI — Service Level Indicator
entries.body: Quantitative measure of one aspect of service level (e.g. success ratio, latency).
entries.snippet: Quantitative measure of one aspect of service level (e.g. success ratio, latency).

entries.title: SLO — Service Level Objective
entries.body: Target value/range for an SLI over a window.
entries.snippet: Target value/range for an SLI over a window.

entries.title: Error budget
entries.body: Allowed unreliability implied by an SLO; guides reliability vs feature investment.
entries.snippet: Allowed unreliability implied by an SLO; guides reliability vs feature investment.

entries.title: GitOps
entries.body: Desired cluster/app state lives in Git; a controller syncs the live system to match.
entries.snippet: Desired cluster/app state lives in Git; a controller syncs the live system to match.

entries.title: Policy-as-code
entries.body: Express admission/security rules as code/config (e.g. Kyverno, Conftest) checked in CI or cluster.
entries.snippet: Express admission/security rules as code/config (e.g. Kyverno, Conftest) checked in CI or cluster.

entries.title: DSL — Domain-Specific Language
entries.body: Mini-language for one problem domain; Challenge Gym deliberately *avoids* inventing one.
entries.snippet: Mini-language for one problem domain; Challenge Gym deliberately *avoids* inventing one.

entries.title: RFC — Request for Comments
entries.body: IETF (and similar) standards documents (e.g. RFC 6238 for TOTP).
entries.snippet: IETF (and similar) standards documents (e.g. RFC 6238 for TOTP).

entries.title: OWASP — Open Worldwide Application Security Project
entries.body: Community publishing practical app-sec guidance (cheat sheets, Juice Shop, etc.).
entries.snippet: Community publishing practical app-sec guidance (cheat sheets, Juice Shop, etc.).

entries.title: NIST — National Institute of Standards and Technology
entries.body: U.S. standards body; SP 800-63 covers digital identity; SP 800-207 covers zero trust architecture.
entries.snippet: U.S. standards body; SP 800-63 covers digital identity; SP 800-207 covers zero trust architecture.

entries.title: STRIDE
entries.body: Threat-category mnemonic: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege.
entries.snippet: Threat-category mnemonic: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege.

entries.title: SAMM — Software Assurance Maturity Model
entries.body: OWASP model for measuring secure-SDLC practices (awareness in this course — not a cert).
entries.snippet: OWASP model for measuring secure-SDLC practices (awareness in this course — not a cert).

entries.title: SDLC — Secure Software Development Life Cycle
entries.body: Building security activities into requirements, design, build, test, and operate.
entries.snippet: Building security activities into requirements, design, build, test, and operate.

entries.title: OSS — Open-source software
entries.body: Software with source available under an open license; contribution practice is an optional stretch here.
entries.snippet: Software with source available under an open license; contribution practice is an optional stretch here.
